newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra may keep analogue network in some rural areas.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra may keep analogue network in some rural areas.

text.p: The Australian government said on Monday the closure of the analogue mobile phone network in 2000 would not disadvantage its rural users.

"We've decided to retain the option of up to five megahertz of spectrum, being left available by way of a residual, in those areas of rural Australia where the digital coverage isn't at least equal to, or better than the city services," Communications Minister Richard Alston said on Monday.
The analogue network is being phased out in favour of digital transmission, which gets more information into its part of the radio frequency spectrum.
But rural communities have little digital coverage and the government has been lobbied to retain the analogue system in those areas.

Alston did not say how the government would protect rural users but he told a National Farmers Federation conference in Canberra that although the competing analogue and digital services were technically quite different it was possible to have a dual-mode handset.
"That would enable you to use the one handset for analogue services in the country and then when you go to the city switch over to a digital service," he said.
Spectrum would be retained in areas where alternative technology, such as global satellite systems, was not available, he said.
But he said ideally he would like to see digital services throughout Australia.
Telecoms carrier Optus has 800,000 analogue customers or one-third of the market, while government-owned carrier Telstra Corp has around 1.8 million customers.
In the digital market, Telstra has about 500,00 customers and Optus has more than 450,000.
